Transition states, IRC and scans¶

This chapter covers reaction paths: relaxed scans, transition-state (TS) searches, intrinsic reaction coordinate (IRC) runs, and the little-documented tasks that take two structures. All of them are driven by the $optimize group. The keywords themselves are described in the reference; this chapter shows how to combine them.

The examples use the isomerization HCN ⇄ HNC and the inversion of ammonia. Unless marked otherwise, they were run on Priroda 25 (2025.02.28) with PBE and the L1 set, and the output excerpts are copied from those runs.

The route¶

A complete study of one elementary step takes six jobs:

  1. Relaxed scan (task=scan) along a coordinate that describes the reaction, to get a rough TS geometry.

  2. Hessian (task=hessian) at the highest point of the scan. It should have an imaginary frequency whose mode is the reaction.

  3. TS search: task=optimize with saddle=1, with the Hessian of step 2 appended to the input as a $Energy group.

  4. Hessian at the TS, to confirm exactly one imaginary frequency.

  5. IRC (task=irc) from the TS with the Hessian of step 4 appended, run twice: once with back=0 and once with back=1.

  6. Re-optimize both IRC endpoints as ordinary minima.

Step 4 is not optional: users report that an IRC started without an accurate Hessian at a converged TS does not work. If you already have a reasonable TS guess from intuition or another program, skip step 1.

The Hessian is passed between jobs as text. Every Hessian run prints a $Energy group on lines prefixed with eng>; strip the prefix and append the last such group to the next input, after $molecule. The command for this is in Getting started (step 6); see also $Energy. If an input holds several $Energy groups, the last one is used, so don’t leave an old one in the file.

All of these tasks ran in version 25 with theory= dft, ridft, rimp2, ccsd, ccsd4t, tddft and qm_n3.

Relaxed scans¶

Input¶

A relaxed scan is a series of constrained optimizations. fix lists the internal coordinates to constrain, five integers each (type, then four atom numbers padded with zeros: 1 distance, 2 angle, 3 dihedral). value gives the start values of all fixed coordinates, then the end values of all of them, in Å and degrees. points is the number of optimizations, both ends included.

This scan turns one H–N–H–H dihedral of ammonia from −180° to −150° in four points, with one N–H bond held at 1.1 Å throughout (its start and end values are equal):

$system mem=256 disk=1 $end
$control
 task=scan
 theory=dft
 basis=/home/user/priroda/basis.in
$end
$optimize
 fix=1,1,2,0,0 3,2,1,4,3
 value=1.1,-180 1.1,-150
 points=4
 tol=1e-5
$end
$molecule
 charge=0 mult=1
 cartesian
 set=L1
   7    0.00000000    0.00000000    0.00000000
   1    0.00000000    0.00000000    1.00800000
   1    0.87295400    0.00000000   -0.50400000
   1   -0.87295400    0.00000000   -0.50400000
$end

The program echoes each constraint with its start and end value:

 constrained variable: type=1 i=  1 j=  2 k=  0 l=  0, value=    1.100000,     1.100000
 constrained variable: type=3 i=  2 j=  1 k=  4 l=  3, value= -180.000000,  -150.000000

Point k of N lies at s = k/(N−1), and every scanned coordinate moves linearly from its start to its end value with s. With points=4 the points are s = 0, 1/3, 2/3 and 1.

Scanning two coordinates¶

Because all coordinates move together with one parameter s, giving two coordinates different start and end values scans them simultaneously, along a straight line in the two-coordinate space, not over a grid. With value=1.0,-180 1.1,-150 in the example above, the N–H bond stretches from 1.0 to 1.1 Å while the dihedral turns.

No source describes a scan over a two-dimensional grid. To map a surface, run one scan per value of the second coordinate, fixing that coordinate with equal start and end values as for the N–H bond above.

Reading the output¶

Each point is an ordinary constrained optimization and ends with OPTIMIZATION CONVERGED in N steps! and its geometry on MOL> lines. After the last point the program repeats all of them under Scan Structures:, each as a line with n, s and E followed by a $molecule group prefixed with SCAN>:

 Scan Structures:
SCAN> n= 0, s=0.000000, E=   -56.40506567
SCAN>$molecule
SCAN> cartesian
SCAN> set=L1
SCAN>   7     0.00000000  -0.00000000  -0.03078317
SCAN>   1    -0.00000000   0.00000000   1.06921683
SCAN>   1     0.87258896  -0.00000000  -0.51921683
SCAN>   1    -0.87258896  -0.00000000  -0.51921683
SCAN>$end

The output ends with a table of E(s) and E(s) − E(0) and a rough text plot of the profile.

To list the points and pull out the geometry of point 1 as a ready $molecule group:

grep '^SCAN> n=' scan.out
awk -v n=1 '/^SCAN> n=/{p=($3==n",")} p&&/^SCAN>\$molecule/{q=1} q{print substr($0,6)} /^SCAN>\$end/{q=0}' scan.out

From the scan maximum to a TS guess¶

The highest point of a scan is only a guess. A relaxed scan can overshoot the barrier and then jump to the other side, so the highest point may be far from the TS and may have no imaginary frequency at all. Compute the Hessian there and check it. The imaginary mode should be the reaction you want; if there is none, or if the imaginary mode is something else (a methyl rotation, say), refine the scan or pick another guess.

For torsions about a double bond (AB C=D EF), a user recommends scanning the twist, the half-sum of the two torsions A–C=D–E and B–C=D–F, rather than a single torsion: the TS lies near a twist of 90°, which is not the same as one torsion at 90°. For a rotation with a symmetric profile, such as the rings of a ferrocene, the same user advises scanning only to locate the TS and then getting the profile from an IRC.

The dihedral sign¶

Priroda’s dihedral angles have the opposite sign to those of Molden, MOPAC, GAMESS and the IUPAC convention. A torsion of +100° in a Priroda Z-matrix is −100° in standard terms. When you take a dihedral value from another program or a molecule viewer, flip its sign before putting it in value=. With the wrong sign, the first scan point is the mirror image of the intended structure (for a chiral or twisted molecule), or a scrambled structure that has nothing in common with the input geometry.

Dihedral values read from a Priroda Z-matrix or Priroda output already have Priroda’s sign. Check the first SCAN> geometry against your input before trusting the rest of a scan.

Transition-state search¶

Input¶

A TS search is an ordinary optimization with saddle=1 and a Hessian in the input. Here is the HCN ⇄ HNC example. First a Hessian at a rough guess, with the hydrogen bridging C and N:

$system mem=256 disk=1 $end
$control
 task=hessian
 theory=dft
 basis=/home/user/priroda/basis.in
$end
$molecule
 charge=0 mult=1
 cartesian
 set=L1
  6      0.000000    0.000000    0.000000
  7      0.000000    0.000000    1.190000
  1      1.132000    0.000000    0.366000
$end

It has one imaginary frequency, 1121.2i cm⁻¹. The TS input is the same with the task changed, an $optimize group added, and the $Energy group of the Hessian run appended after $molecule:

$control
 task=optimize
 theory=dft
 basis=/home/user/priroda/basis.in
$end
$optimize saddle=1 steps=100 $end

What the output confirms¶

Before the first step, the optimizer echoes its settings and reports the lowest eigenvalues of the Hessian it read:

 Geometry optimization options:
 Coordinates: internal
 Tolerance on gradient       = 0.00010000
 Tolerance on displacement   = 0.01000000
 Trust radius                = 0.12500000 (max), 0.01562500 (min)
 Maximum number of steps     =        100
 Updated hessian used
 Saddle point search: follow = 1

 Geometry Optimization Step 0:
     9 cartesian,    3 internal coordinates
     3 independent variables
 include g
 Lowest eigenvalues: -0.33562  0.28349
 chosen: -0.33562

Check three things here:

  • Saddle point search: follow = 1 shows that saddle=1 was read.

  • Lowest eigenvalues: with one negative value shows that the appended Hessian was read and has the right shape. If both values are positive, the Hessian is wrong for this geometry (in a test with the minimum’s Hessian appended instead, the search ran all 128 steps without converging).

  • chosen: names the eigenvalue whose eigenvector the search climbs.

The run ends like any optimization, with OPTIMIZATION CONVERGED in 3 steps! and the TS geometry on MOL> lines. The step limits are those of an ordinary optimization: trust, steps and tolerance. The sources give no TS-specific advice on them.

Confirm one imaginary frequency¶

Run task=hessian at the converged TS. The frequency table marks imaginary frequencies with a trailing i:

 | Mode | Freq.   | Mass.  | IR Int. |Raman A. |Raman D.| ROA (90)  | ROA (180) |
 *------*---------*--------*---------*---------*--------*-----------*-----------*
 |    1 | 1090.23i|   1.16 |  76.020 |   0.000 | 0.0000 |   0.00000 |   0.00000 |

Exactly one imaginary frequency, whose mode (printed under Normal Modes, or viewed in Molden with print=+molden) moves the atoms along the reaction, means a TS. Keep this output: its $Energy group is the input Hessian for the IRC.

Several imaginary frequencies¶

If the Hessian of the guess has more than one imaginary frequency, or the lowest one is not the reaction, the search may climb the wrong mode. follow selects which Hessian eigenvector to follow (the default is the first); check the chosen: line to see which one was taken. One user who followed a chosen mode reports that it works best when the Hessian shows that mode clearly. Often the better fix is a better guess: refine the scan near the maximum, or displace the geometry along the unwanted mode and recompute the Hessian.

Note

On very flat surfaces, such as a methyl rotation with a frequency of a few cm⁻¹, users warn that stationary points may be artifacts, and that a stationary point found with one method can lie somewhere else entirely with another. A scan is often more informative there than a TS search.

IRC¶

Input¶

The IRC input holds the TS geometry (the MOL> group of the TS search) and the $Energy group of the Hessian at the TS:

$system mem=256 disk=1 $end
$control
 task=irc
 theory=dft
 basis=/home/user/priroda/basis.in
$end
$optimize points=30 back=0 $end
$molecule
 cartesian
 set=L1
   6    -0.38764722   0.00000000  -0.52922493
   7    -0.35863431   0.00000000   0.66492317
   1     0.74628153   0.00000000  -0.13569824
$end

Each run follows the path in one direction only. Run it a second time with back=1 for the other direction. points is the maximum number of IRC points; the run stops earlier when it reaches a minimum. In the HCN example 30 was enough: the halves took 19 and 21 points.

radius sets the step, in mass-weighted coordinates; adjacent points end up about twice the radius apart. The default (0.1 in version 25) worked for both ammonia inversion and the hydrogen shift in HCN. A smaller radius gives more points and a path that ends closer to the minimum, at higher cost; a larger one gives fewer points and ends farther away. Dft.rtf gives an older default of 0.2.

Reading the output¶

The header repeats the direction, the radius and the imaginary mode:

 Intrinsic Reaction Coordinate
 -----------------------------
 n = 1, back = 0, down = 1
 r = 0.1000000000
 frequency = 1089.34i cm^-1:

Point 0 is a single point at the TS. Every further point is a constrained optimization (Constrained Optimization for Path Point  N:) that ends with OPTIMIZATION CONVERGED and prints the point’s distance from the TS, energy and gradient, then its geometry on IRC> lines:

IRC> point   1: distance =   0.19448552 E =   -93.26282908 g = 0.00857678
IRC>$molecule
IRC> cartesian
IRC> set=L1
IRC>   6    -0.37714562   0.00000000  -0.52170012
IRC>   7    -0.36950686   0.00000000   0.66925190
IRC>   1     0.76111634   0.00000000  -0.21389325
IRC>$end

With back=1 the distances are negative. At the end the program prints REACTION PATH: and lists the points again, ordered by distance, so the back=1 list runs from the far end towards the TS.

How an IRC ends¶

Two messages end a normal IRC:

  • Vicinity of a Stationary Point(?) --- STOP.: the path has reached the region of a minimum (the gradient has become small).

  • Energy Minimum Passed --- STOP.: the last point came out higher than the one before, so the path has stepped over the minimum. It often follows the Vicinity message.

 Vicinity of a Stationary Point(?) --- STOP.
IRC> point  19: distance =   3.73559541 E =   -93.33987986 g = 0.00571851
...
 Energy Minimum Passed --- STOP.

The Vicinity message on the first step is not a normal end; see the pitfalls below. An IRC can also stop before points is reached on a flat shelf or at another TS.

Note

In the version 25 test outputs, the point printed after a Vicinity stop was sometimes missing from the REACTION PATH: list. Take endpoint geometries from the last IRC> groups before that list, not only from the list.

Joining the two halves¶

The official site has a small shell script, grx, that copies the REACTION PATH sections of two IRC outputs into one file:

sed -n '/REAC/,$p' irc_back1.out  > irc.txt
sed -n '/REAC/,$p' irc_back0.out >> irc.txt

grx irc_back1.out irc_back0.out irc.txt does the same, after checking that both files contain REACTION PATH and that irc.txt does not exist yet. Give the back=1 output first: its list ends at the TS and the back=0 list starts there, so the joined file runs in order of distance from one minimum through the TS to the other (point 0 appears twice).

Re-optimize the endpoints¶

An IRC ends near a minimum, not in it. Take the last IRC> geometry of each half and optimize it, best with task=optimize+hessian so that the Hessian confirms a minimum. This extracts the last geometry:

sed -n '1,/REACTION PATH/p' irc_back0.out |
  awk '/^IRC>\$molecule/{b="";q=1} q{b=b substr($0,5) "\n"} /^IRC>\$end/{q=0} END{printf "%s",b}' > end0.mol

Put end0.mol in place of the $molecule group of an input with task=optimize+hessian, and do the same for the back=1 output.

If an endpoint turns out to be another TS or a shelf, compute a Hessian there and run a new IRC from it.

Tasks that take two structures¶

Three tasks start from two $molecule groups, the start and the end structure, with the atoms numbered the same way in both. They are hardly documented; treat them as experimental.

Task

What it does

Status

saddle

“Approximate Saddle Point Search”: a one-dimensional maximization between the two structures, then a two-dimensional saddle search

Runs in version 25

transit

“Synchronous Transit in Internal Coordinates”

Reported working in version 8; crashed in version 25

path

“Minimum Energy Path Optimization”

No test and no usage report

For the two mirror images of pyramidal ammonia, task=saddle printed Stage 1: One-Dimensional Maximization:, stopped at the planar midpoint (s = 0.5, E = −56.4876815, against −56.4877160 for the fully optimized TS), then Stage 2: Two-Dimensional Saddle Point Search:, and ended normally. The input is two complete $molecule groups after $control:

$system mem=256 disk=1 $end
$control
 task=saddle
 theory=dft
 basis=/home/user/priroda/basis.in
$end
$molecule
 charge=0 mult=1
 cartesian
 set=L1
  7    0.000000    0.000000    0.110000
  1    0.000000    0.940000   -0.260000
  1    0.814064   -0.470000   -0.260000
  1   -0.814064   -0.470000   -0.260000
$end
$molecule
 charge=0 mult=1
 cartesian
 set=L1
  7    0.000000    0.000000   -0.110000
  1    0.000000    0.940000    0.260000
  1    0.814064   -0.470000    0.260000
  1   -0.814064   -0.470000    0.260000
$end

Use the result as a TS guess and continue with a Hessian and saddle=1 as above.

Warning

task=transit with the same input printed the internal coordinates of both structures and then crashed with Bus error in version 25. Users found it useful in version 8 for generating a TS guess when the reactive mode is unclear, and found task=saddle about twice as fast on the same problem.

Two further task names appear in older program banners: conical (“Conical intersection (0,1)”) and extremal (“Calculation of Gradient Extremal Path”, slow). Neither has been tested and no usage is reported; a forum question about conical intersections in Priroda went unanswered.

Pitfalls¶

  • An IRC from a geometry that is not a converged TS gives only a couple of points, or no path at all. Always run steps 3 and 4 of the route first.

  • Vicinity of a Stationary Point(?) on the first IRC step means the energy did not go down on that step. Change radius: larger on a very flat barrier top, smaller on a narrow barrier such as a proton transfer.

  • A scan that starts from a mangled geometry almost always has a dihedral with the wrong sign (see The dihedral sign).

  • TDDFT scans: coordinates that are not fixed relax on the excited-state surface and can dissociate. In a version 25 test the excited-state iterations then gave nan and the run stopped; fixing all three N–H bonds made the same scan converge.

  • A Hessian from a different method or basis: gradient=0 is meant for this case. Version 25 TS searches with ridft, rimp2, ccsd and tddft converged from a DFT Hessian without it.

  • Two task= lines do not chain jobs: version 25 runs only the last one. Run scan, Hessian, TS search and IRC as separate jobs.

More on these problems is in Geometry optimization problems and the IRC sections that follow it in Solving common problems.
